description.p: BIOLOGICALLY COMPATIBLE TAMPON SPONGE Background of the Invention This invention relates to methods of production of three-dimensional polymer structures, and to the use of such structures as medical devices.

One embodiment of the invention is a contraceptive which has the potential to help alleviate the problem of over population. This application of the invention is of such immense importance that it deserves special discussion throughout.

Social scientists recognize that over population is one of the most serious problems which mankind must face and solve. As an example, in the United States the Department of Health, Education and Welfare released statistics recently which showed that 3.3 million babies were born in the United States in 1977, up 5% from the previous year. This marked an increase in the nation's birth rate for the first time since 1970. (1) The .problem is even more critical in underdeveloped countries. In order to control our increasing world population, there exists a myriad of contraceptive devices to prevent unwanted pregnancy.

Each method attempts to achieve a contraceptive possessing the qualities of simplicity, acceptability, efficacy, nontoxicity and absence of adverse side effects. One class of such measures are mechanical contraceptives, such as the diaphragm -, which are inserted into the vagina to completely occlude the orafice of the cervix, thus obstructing the migration of spermatozoa upward into the fallopian tubes. Such contraceptives have serious application problems due to the wide variation in size and geometry of the vaginal canal and the cervical opening. These devices often require special insertion instruments and careful fitting, usually by a trained physician.

Furthermore, since trained help in application is often necessary, these devices are ill-suited for the underdeveloped countries where they are needed most.
Chemical or spermicidal contraceptives are another well known method for attempting to prevent pregnancy. These devices consist of a carrier agent such as jellies and creams which provide partial obstruction of the cervix and in addition contain nontoxic chemical agents that immobilize sperm. The creams and jellies can be inserted high into the vagina with an applicator or can be encapsulated as capsules or suppositories. Capsules or suppositories are placed in the vagina shortl before coitus to allow sufficient time for them to melt -and disperse their active ingredients. However, the use of these devices have resulted in unwanted pregnancie because the spermicidal material is not held for a sufficient length of time (which may be several hours) ' in the desired location in relation to the cervical opening. As a result of this inability to be effective alone, creams and jellies are often used in conjunction with other contraceptive devices. In addition, supposito require skill in positioning the device in the depth of the vagina in order to prevent flow back out the vaginal opening.

Another type of mechanical device is the condom, a rubber device that surrounds the penis and contains the sperm after ejaculation. This widely used device suffers from an unnatural or desensitizing feeling to the male and female. In addition, the possibility of a perforation in the sheath and the problem of disposing of spent condoms, make the device less than the ultimate answer to unwanted pregnancy.

Recently, oral contraceptives have gained prominence. The "pill" is a female contraceptive which works by suppressing ovulation. One type of "pill" contains a combination of estrogen and progestogen. The Food and Drug Administration has recently published a brochure which reports that estrogen causes cancer in som animals, but studies have not confirmed that it causes
cancer in humans. This brochure also states that the pill doubles a woman's chance of having a heart attack as well as increasing the risk of other circulatory problems.

Risk of heart attack is further increased if the woman is a smoker. Pill users who smoke are three times more likely to die of a heart attack than nonsmokers on the pill and ten times more likely than nonsmokers who do not use the pill. (2)

The pill should not be taken by females who have certain ailments. In addition, undesirable side effects will sometimes occur when the female first takes the oral contraceptive. These include nausea and vomiting, increase in breast tenderness and engorgement, accentuation of acne, fluid retention, weight gain, increased vaginal discharge and breakthrough bleeding. Finally, there is documentation to the effect that the risk of death to the user may be on the order of 3 per 100,000. (3) Some pharmacological research* has been focused recently upon producing male oral contraceptives. Alkylating agents and hormones to regulate spermatogenesis and thereby bring about a temporary or controlled sterility have been the subject of experimentation. However, alkylating agents are considered dangerous due to possible irreversible side effects and toxicity. Many unanswered questions remain with the use of hormones also. (4)

In order to obviate some of the above deficiencies there have been attempts to combine mechanical and chemical contraceptive properties into a single device through the use of polymeric matrices carrying a pharmaceutically active amount of spermicide.

One such attempt is disclosed in U.S. Patent No. 3,261,353 by T.H. Johnson. Johnson teaches a device consisting of a laminate which contains a spermicide. The laminate consists of a nonporous rubber sheet
cemented to a porous rubber or polymer foam. The spermicide is used in an amount ranging from 1 to 10% and is applied to the rubber or plastic foam through compression between rollers which may be enhanced by a surface application as by painting or dipping.

This device possesses several deficiencies however. For example, the need for a nonporous rubber sheet cemente to the polymer foam creates a device lacking the desired flexibility and natural feeling desired. Secondly, the foam contains a relatively low percentage of spermicide (1-10%). Thirdly, the spermicide would have a short retention time in the polymer foam.
A different approach to the problem is illustrated in U.S. Patent No. 3,514,517 issued to Furuse et al.

Furuse teaches as one aspect of the invention the formati of a suppository from various surfactant/spermicides and polyethylene glycol. This process produces a suppository which melts and dissolves in the vaginal canal. U.S. Patent No. 3,903,232 issued to Wood et al is directed to a foam structure which is prepared by using a isocyanate capped polyoxyethylene polyol reacted with large amounts of water. This specific polymer has been found to produce stable hydrophilic foams which are easil compressed, but which expand back to their original shape. Such foams contain a biocide, which upon contact with water is released. This enables such foams to be extreme useful for washing, wiping, cleaning the external body or used internally such as in the form of a tampon. However it has been found that while the foam-like structure prod under the Wood et al method is extremely useful, such structure does' not retain the biocide materials any great length of time and thus, the sponge has limited long term applicability. The present invention is an improvement in the art of manufacturing sponge-like structures which can have a pharmaceutically active ingredient contained therein and
which contain none of the shortcomings discussed herein- above in connectiqn with the prior art. The present invention enables a sponge-like structure to be formed which is flexible and which can be molded into a wide range of various shapes and sizes but which permits the retention of a pharmaceutically active agent therein for great lengths of time. Because of this feature, the sponge produced according to the present invention has distinct advantages in terms of an intravaginal device to be used by women in the treatment of vaginal disorders , s well as birth control device. A sponge produced under the present invention could be used in the vagina for a period of up to one month, and yet still be biologically active in terms of either permitting the timed release application of medication or the retention of a spermicide to improve the device's effectiveness as a contraceptive.

Summary of the Invention A medical device, method of manufacture and packaging which will obviate the deficiencies in the prior art have been discovered and are disclosed. The device is a tampon polymer sponge containing a pharmaceutical agent which also acts as a surfactant/ foaming agent for the polymer. The surprising synergis ic result obtained from the polymer agent combination together with the unique method of manufacture and packaging produce a medical device possessing all of the following properties:
(1) A simple device which can be inserted in privacy without a special applicator or counsel of a physician.
(2) A biocompatible, nontoxic, nonirritating device with no adverse side effects.
(3) As a contraceptive, a device which is so natural and soft in feeling that neither sexual partner is aware of its presence.

(4) As a contraceptive, a reuseable device with long lasting spermicidal activity, a factor of
immense importance in underdeveloped countries.
(5) As a contraceptive, an effective vaginal contraceptive' which need not be used in conjunctio with creams, jellies or other suppositories.
(6) A device which is unitarily packaged in situ in a simple, completely sanitary reuseable container.

As a contraceptive, the 'sponge possesses the mecha properties of blocking the cervical opening when inserte and also of absorbing sperm through the porous cells. In addition, it possesses a" chemical property by slowly releasing a spermicide.

The sponge is formed by mixing a polymeric materia or a monomor or prepolymer thereof with an aqueous solu of the pharmaceutical agent surfactant. After mixing, the blend is poured into a cavity polymer mold where it begins to foam. If the pharmaceutical agent is in large enough amounts, i.e., greater than 10% by dry weight of sponge, it serves the critical function as a foaming ag which decreases the pore size of the resulting polymer foam. If the pharmaceutical agent is in an amount less than 10% of the dry weight of the sponge, an organic fibril such as collagen must be added to help encapsula the agent. This method which is a further embodiment of the invention, comprises the steps of forming an aqueous collagen slurry of acid-swollen collagen fibers which can include a pharmaceutically active agent. The collagen fibrils are mixed with the water so as to be substantially uniformly distributed in the slurry and comprise up to about 10 weight percent and preferably 0.1 to 10 weight percent of the slurry. The collagen slurry is then mixed, preferably with a water-catalyzed urethane prepolymer, and the ratio of collagen slurry t urethane prepolymer of 2:1 to 4:1. These ratios can be increased depending on technique (e.g., pH adjustmen used to decrease the viscosity of the collagen slurry thereby enabling efficient mixing of the slurry with
the polymer. Increasing this ratio increases the percentage of collagen in the final sponge composite. The weight percent of collagen fibrils in the final sponge is preferably up to 40 weight percent. After thoroughly mixing the collagen slurry with the prepolymer, the mixture is poured or injected under pressure into a mold so as to permit the continued reaction of the polyurethane prepolymer which foams into a stable, but flexible sponge-like structure with the foam substantially encapsulating the collagen fibrils and the pharmaceutically active agent. The resulting sponge is durable and has tear and fatigue strengths exceeding that of the prior art collagen sponges. Without the presence of the surfactant or collagen the physical characteristics of the sponge would drastically differ, probably the most important difference being that the pore size of the sponge would be too large to retain a pharmaceutical agent for any appreciable period. As the foa ing is near completion the mold is closed and sealed and the mold thus becomes the package in which the device is commercially sold. This unique packaging procedure insures a completely sanitary product.

The novel features which are believed to be characteris- tic of the invention, both as to its organization and method of operation, together with further objectives and advantages thereof, will be better understood from the following description considered in connection with the accompanying drawings in which a presently preferred embodiment of the invention is illustrated by way of examples. It is to be expressly understood, however, that the drawings are for the purpose of illustration and description only and are not intended as a definition of the limits of the invention. Description of the Preferred Embodiment

Broadly, this invention is directed to a method for forming a three-dimensional sponge-like structure having particular utility in the medical arts. Referring first to Figures 1 and 2, one can see a prior art polymeric sponge 10 with the various pore-like structure 12 formed therein by the cross linking of the various polymeric chains 14. While a sponge made entirely of a polymeric foam without any pharmaceutically active agent is not within the scope of this invention, the type of stable polymeric foam which has been found to be particularly useful in this invention is the type of urethane foam described in U.S. Patent No. 3,903,232 and herein
incorporated by reference.

The interstitial spaces 16, as shown in Figure 2, formed by the cross linking of the various polymeric chains 14 are believed to provide the sponge with its unique flexing characteristic. However, it is believed that because the spaces 16 are relatively wide open, most types of pharmaceutically active materials in the sponge 10 would quickly be removed therefrom and this, any prolonged biological activity would not remain. Accordingly, the use of pure urethane sponges as internal medical devices for supplying the user with a pharmaceutical agent has not been well received.

Reference is now made to -Figures 3 and 4 which show a pure collagen sponge 18 as having a rather tight-knot pore structure -and having a general homogeneous appearance without the visible pores as shown with reference to the sponge in Figure 1. The collagen sponge 18 as shown in the enlarged view in Figure 4, has a plurality of collagen fibers 20 which are joined to general masses 22 of collagen material. As discussed hereinabove, such sponges are expensive to make, are somewhat flexible, and furthermore, do not -retain pharmaceutically active agents for extended periods. Referring now to Figures 5. and 6,.the sponge 24 of the present invention is shown. As indicated in Figure 5, the sponge has a generally uniform appearance with a small cellular structure. In Figure 6, however, the cells 26 are shown as having the collagen fibrils 28 disposed therein. The fibrils in turn have the pharmaceu¬ tically active agent/surfactant absorbed in them and thus, when the sponge 24 is flexed, the fibrils 28 exude the pharmaceutical agent/surfactant which then flows out through the cellular structure 26. In this manner, the agent/surfactant remains in the sponge 24 for extended period of time, but does so in a controlled manner.
Referring now to Figure 7 , one can see the various collagen fibrils 28 in their extended configuration. This extended confirguration is achieved by disbursing such fibrils in water o other liquid. When in this extended configuration , the collagen fibers 28 can absorb a relatively large quantity of pharmaceutically active agent. Unless such fibrils 28 are extended, they tend to clump up and would only be able to absorbe relatively little pharmaceutical agent. Thus , as hereinbelow described, one embodiment of the present invention calls for a slurry formed of collagen fibrils rather than the addition of collagen fibrils per se to the polymeric material . Figure 9 illustrates a tampon sponge 30 without collagen but with greater than 10% by dry weight of the pharmaceutical agent. A polymeric sponge structure 32 is shown with tiny pores 34 which are in communication with the sponge's inner structure (not shown). A flexible loop, 36, is attached to the structure 32 to provide a convenient removal means. * *

Polymeric sponge structure 32 is a soft pliable porous sponge in the shape of a flattened ball with a diameter of approximately two inches. Prefer.ably, the foam structure is prepared by using a polyurethane prepolymer reacted with large amounts of water. The preferred prepolymer is an isocy-anate capped polyoxytheylene polyol.

It is expressly understood, however, that while the polyurethane prepolymer described hereinabove is the preferred polymeric material, other polymers are clearly within the scope of this invention. For example, ethylene vinyl acetate copolymers, polyethylene oxide/polyethylene terephthalate copolymers, as well, as all other biologically inert and non-skin irritating polymers, as well as the prepolymer and monomer thereof are clearly within the scope of this invention so long as such polymers will produ
a flexible sponge-like foam mater a .

The polyoxyethylene polyol used as--a reactant in preparing the* capped product to be foamed into the sponge of the present invention may have a weight average molecular weight of about 200 to 1500, with a hydroxyϊ functionality of three or greater. The polyoxyethylene polyol is terminated or capped by reaction with a polyisocyanate. The reaction may be carried out in an inert moisture-free atmosphere, such as under a nitrogen blanket at. atmospheric pressure at a temperature in the range of 0° to about 120°C for a period of about twenty hours depending on the temperature and degree of agitation. The polyisocyanates used for capping the polyoxyethylene polyol include the various polyisocyanates set forth in the Wood et al disclosure.

Capping of the polyoxyethylene polyol may be effected using stoichometric amounts of reactants. Desirably, however, an excess of isocyanate is used to insure complete capping of the polyol. Thus, the ratio of isocyanate groups to the hydroxyl groups used for capping is between about 1 to about 4 isocyanate to hydroxyl molar ratio.
Water soluble or water dispersable biologically cross linking agents could be used in forming the prepolymer.

Citric acid is one such possible cross linking agent which the present invention has incorporated albeit for other purposes than functioning as a cross linking agent, described later. However, the use of cross linking agents should be carefully considered inasmuch as the sponge of the present invention is to be used internally. Cross linking agents, such as the polyamines, i.e., triethylene amine or diaminotoluene are known irritants and therefore should be avoided. The foaming and preparation of the sponge structure will be described for the embodiment as a contraceptive as follows:
A solution of water -containing various additives including the spermicide/surfactant is mixed with a solution of the urethane prepolymer. The ratio of polymer to water is in the range of 30-150 parts by weight polymer to 100 parts by weight water. Conversely, the ratio of water to polymer is 66-133 parts by weight water to 100 parts by weight polymer. If either an excess or a deficie of water is present, an incomplete, reaction results. In the preferred embodiment, 77.77 parts of the polymer - are mixed with 100 parts water in order that: the volume ratios would result with two volumes of water to one volume of polymer.- This 2:1 volume ratio, which is exemplary only, was chosen for convenience in order that in the manufacturing process two units of water could be added to one unit of polymer solution.

The final optimum ratios in parts by weight are: 4.5 parts water, 1.5 parts spermicide and 3.5 parts urethane prepolymer. This gives the above indicated volume ratio for the water to prepolymer of 2:1.

The aqueous solution contains the spermicide/surfacta One of the unexpected and surprising discoveries embodied in this invention is the synergistic combination of a pharmaceutical agent which also serves the function a surfactant with a polyurethane prepolymer. One such age surfactant is nonylphenoxypoly (ethyleneoxy) ethanol, here referred to as nonoxynol 9 which is a spermicide commonly used in vaginal birth control foam, gels and creams. Othe examples of such spermicide surfactants which could be equivalent are p-menthanyl phenylpolyoxyethylene ether, nonyl phenylpolyoxynylethylene ether, octyl cresolpolyoxyethylene ether, polyoxyethylene oxypropylene stearate, polyoxyethylene laurate, glycerol ricinolate, di-iso-butyl phenylpolyoxyethylene ether, tri-isopropyl phenylpolyoxyethylene ether, mono-iso-octyl phenyl ether polyethylene glycol, methoxy polyoxyethylene glycol 500 laureate, polyoxyethylene stearyla ine, benzalconium
chloride , cetyl tri ethylammonium bromide , methyl benzetonium chloride , benzetonium chloride , methyl dodecylxylyrene-bis- trimethylammonium chloride , sodium dodecylsulfate , di-ethylhexyl sodium sulfosuccinate , nonylphenolpolyethylene sodium sulfate , sodium oleate , zincphenolsulfonate , . dodecylbenzen sulfonate , dodecyl diaminoethyl-gl cine and the like .

The acceptable percentage of pharmaceutical agent in the sponge is greater than 10% and less than 50% dry weight of the sponge, preferably 20%-40% and optimumly 30%. The formulation of these percentages is a highly surprising discovery and resulted from rigorous experimentation. The high percentages of pharmaceutical agent/surfactant present in the claimed invention are unusual because heretofore it was well known that in producing polymer foams it is desirable to use as little surfactant as possible in order to maintain the purity of the resulting polymeric -foam. However, it was found that the use of these surfactants in percentages of 10% or less produced foams which did not retain the agent for any appreciable period. The agents were quickly washed out of the sponge.

Reference is now made to Figure 8 which is a graph comparing the amount of pharmaceutically active agent released per gram of sponge with the number of washings of the sponge. In making this graph, two sponges were prepared with the only difference being in that one sponge contained 12 weight percent collagen, while the other sponge contained no collagen. However, both sponges contain approximately the same amount of pharmaceutically active agent/surfactant but less than 10% by dry weight. As shown in said graph, the sponge without the collagen had 90.7% of its pharmaceutically active agent/surfactant washed out after twenty washings. The sponge with 12% collagen had much improved retention of the pharmaceutically active agent/ surfactant and had only 23% of such ingredient washed out after twenty washings.
It has now been discovered that in order to eliminate the need for organic fibrils such as collagen, the surfact concentration has to be increased in order to decrease the polymeric cellular foam s i ze thereby increas ing the ' sponge ' capacity to retain the pharmaceutical agent . In fact , the percentage of surfactant used is directly proportional to a decrease in the cellular pore size of the sponge . The following conclusions can be obtained from the spermicidal effectiveness test:
(1) At least 30% of the nonoxynol 9 is required if the sponge is likely to be washed and reused.
(2) There appears to be a sharp increase in spermicidal effectiveness and longevity between 20% nonoxynol 9 and 30% nonoxynol 9.
(3) A sponge containing 30% nonoxynol 9 retains spermicidal effectiveness through 15 rinses.
(4) Addition of preservations and a pH reducer (citric acid) alone or combined have little, if any, effect on spermicidal action.
(5) Addition of preservatives increases spermicidal action slightly.
(6) Addition of a pH reducer (citric acid) increases spermicidal action slightly.

It was found that if the percentage of pharmaceutical agent rises above 50%, the sponge will become quite viscous and sticky which is of course an unacceptable condition. Thus, by increasing the dry weight percentages of pharmaceutical agent to up to 50% and preferably around

30%, an extraordinary amount of agent is available in the sponge and the cellular pore size in the sponge is decreased sufficiently to produce a sponge with a great capacity to retain the agent. This decrease in cellular pore size in the sponge has made it unnecessary to include an additive such as collagen which is quite an important result since collagen presents several problems from a quality control standpoint, i.e. , purification, etc.

Several additives may optionally be added to the water solution in addition to the pharmaceutical agent. For example, various preservatives, antifungicide, antibacterial agents and antioxidents may be added. Also, pH adjusters and buffers may be added. In the preferred embodiment a mixture of distilled water, and distilled, deionized demineralized water is mixed with 1/10 of 1% of
benzoic acid, 2/10 of 1% of sorbic* acid, 1/10 of 1% of sodium hydroxide, 2% of monhydrate citric acid and 5/100 of 1% of sodium metabisulphite. The benzoic acid and sorbic act as preservatives . to prevent bacterial or fungus growth from occuring especially when the sponge might be stored after use.

The citric acid is used to lower the pH of the solution to about 3.5. This is done to conform the sponge pH to the pH in the vaginal range which is approximately 4.0 to 5.0. If the vaginal pH is increased to much above that range, bacteria can begin to grow. For ex-ample, the gonococcus bacillus is very fragile and dies at low pH after only a short period of time. Another reason for dropping the pH to a more acidic level in the contraceptive embodiment is that an acid environment is hostile to sperm and will decrease the sperm motility eventually to total incapacitation. The citric acid is then buffered with sodium hydroxide. The sodium hydroxide reacts with the citric acid to give a sodium dihydrogen citrate which provides the buffer action without reducing the citric acid content significantly. Another possible buffer which could be used is sodium citrate, but the sodium hydroxide is preferable. The sodium metabisulphite serves as an antiσxidant thereby depressing any oxidation processes which might occur.
This additive solution is given to disclose the preferred embodiment. Acceptable ranges for these additives can be found in the following publications: Remington

Pharmaceutical Sciences, 15th Edition, 1975, published by Mack Publishing Company; the Martindale Pharmacopoeia, published by the Pharmaceutical Press in London; the United States Pharmacoppeiar published by the United States Pharmacopoeia Convention, Inc.; and the Merck Index, published by Merck and Company, entirely and yet stay within the framework of the claimed invention.
In addition, collagen fibers may be added to the solution in order to further aid in forming a sponge which will retain the pharmaceutical agent. In order to make the acid swollen collagen fibrils used in the present invention, the general procedures as described in U.S. Patent Nos. 3,123,482 and 3,114,593 are used and which references are herein incorporated by reference. The specific method of manufacturing acid swollen collagen fibrils does not play an important aspect of the present invention and thus , will not be described in detail herein. Basically, however, the method comprises the steps of obtaining a collagen mass obtained through alkaline and/or acidic decomposition of beef hides or beef tendons mechanically comminuted which is washed several times with a ten percent sodium chloride solution in order to remove impurities. The washed collagen mass is then suspended in water and the pH values adjusted to above 4, preferably from 4 to 5. This collagen mass or paste, with a collagen content of about 8 to 20 (dry weight basis) is then treated with so much water and with other materials, such as surfactants, pharmaceutically active agents, pH adjusters, viscosity indexers, and the like, as desired that the collagen content of the obtained mixture or slurry (dry weight basis) is 0.1 to 10%, preferably 0.5 to 2%, where upon the obtained slurry is then mixed with the polymeric material as hereinbelo described.

Further, tanning agents, such as glutaraldehyde, may be incorporated into the collagen slurry before mixing with the prepolymer. Such tanning agents employed in various concentrations will result in cross linking of the collagen fibers giving additional structural strength to the composite sponge.

The conclusions that are obtained from the experiments depicted in Table C are as follows:
(1) Increasing percentages of nonoxynol 9 decreases the pH to more acidic levels.

As stated earlier, two volumes of the water additive solution are mixed with one volume of the urethane prepolymer. This mixture is effected by a high shear mixer which produces a creaming action and the solution is ready to be poured or injected into a mold to begin its foaming action. The prepolymer can optionally be heated to temperatures of approximately 110 to 120°F. These higher temperatures lower the cell density of the resulting sponge making the resulting sponge more porous and easier to handle. A further, and extremely important, aspect of the claimed invention is the method of manufacture of the end product polymer sponge and its packaging. It is critical in this type of product that the product be packaged in sanitary containers. This is often difficult where a product has to be handled after its manufacture. The packaging and sanitization problem has been solved by molding the sponge in a polymer mold preferably having two cavities. Referring to Figure 10, two halves of the mold are shown as an upper half 38 and a lower half 40. The material and surface finish of the mold are important in several respects.

First, the surface of the mold is critical in forming the exterior characteristics of the sponge. For example, n forming the sponge upon foaming, there is a tendency for the sponge to form a shiny skinlike surface on its exterior. This is quite undesirable in the contraceptive
embodiment, for the reasons that the sponge will not absorb the sperm as well nor will it release the spermicide through its outer pores as well, It has now been discovered that polypropylene or polyallomer are acceptable polymers in formation of the mold. The polyallomer which is a polymer manufactured by Eastman Chemical Products, Inc., Plastics Division, Kingsport, Tennessee, has been found to be especially advantageous particularly in view of the fact that it is generally recognized as safe as used in intravenous solution bottles. Both the polypropylene and polyallomer have been found to be successful in preventing any skin formation on the contraceptive sponge.

Secondly, and probably more important than the actual material of the mold, the surface finish of the mold must not be smooth. A smooth finish will produce a sponge with a shiny skin. However, a certain finish which is about 60 grit i.e., the finish resulting from use of a 60 grit sandblast, provides a rough finish which will prevent any skin formation. The premixed urethane-water-pharmaceutical agent solution is poured into the two halves of the mold. The foam forms by spontaneous exothermic reaction filling the mold cup. Just before the mold cups are filled, a soft dacron ribbon loop 36 as shown in Figure 11 is laid over one half of the mold 38 and the other half is quickly closed over half 38 with the loop inbetween.

With the mold closed, the polymer continues to foam with the air escaping out through a crack around the middle of the mold so that no air bubbles are trapped in the sponge. The shot size of material poured into the mold is measured precisely so that the sponge will just fill the container. The air escapes through the mold seam as the foam blows but the.polymer solution will not escape since it is more viscous than the air. Shortly after the foaming operation is completed, perhaps 5 or 10 minutes later, a shrink wrap is placed over the outside of the container. The package is then placed in an oven which shrinks that outer wrapping so that there is a tight seal and the product is now ready to be
commercially sold, as shown in Figure 12. The mold therefore forms the final package and the product is thereby never removed from the mold. This produces a completely sanitary container.

The loop 36 on the sponge allows the tampon,to be easily grasped for removal from the vaginal canal. The removal loop is made from 100% woven polyester which is a soft weave, non-irritating, and biocompatible. The loops are welded into circular shape with an ultrasonic weld.

Example 1

2,300 grams of collagen paste are mixed in a high shear blender with 4,600 grams of distilled water to which have been added 200 grams of nonpxynol-9 surfactant/spermic With the temperature of the HYPOL FHP 2001 (trade name for the isocyanate capped hydrophilic polyoxyethylene polyol, manufactured by W. R. Grace & Company, 55 Hayden Avenue, Lexington, Massachusetts 02173) at 110°, two parts of the room temperature collagen slurry were mixed with one part o the FHP 2001.

Samples were mixed in a high shear mixer (Martin Sweets Co. Flexamatic 30-H) so as to produce a creaming act and were poured into a mold where upon cross linking of the urethane resulted in approximately 2 to 3 minutes, yielding a tack-free, but flexible, three-dimensional foam-like urethan/collagen structure, with collagen comprising about 12% by weight of the dry sponge.
Example 2 The following procedure was repeated as set forth in Example 1 except the temperature of the FHP 2001 was raised to 120°F and a second foam-like structure of lower . density was obtained.
Example 3 The same prodecure was repeated as in Example 1, but the ratio of slurry to urethane was changed to 4:1, resulting in a higher percentage (15.5%) of collagen in the dry sponge.
Example 4 This example consisted of FHP 2011 (without the collagen) in equal parts by weight to the following mix:

3 liters of water, 60 grams of nonoxynol-9 and 60 grams of zinc sulfate.
Example 5

In this example, the collagen slurry, the nonoxynol-9 and the water were mixed in a high-speed "Waring" blender. 20 parts slurry, 80 parts water, and 2 parts nonoxynol-9 were used. To this room temperature slurry, 20 parts FHP 2001 were added and mixed by hand using a laboratory mixing spatula. Excellent creaming resulted in a matter of seconds, and after pouring into simple molds of various shapes, uniform tack-free composite sponges were demolded in about 3 minutes.
Results:
Example

2 Properties similar to those of Example 1 were obtained, except that low density resulted from increased blowing of the urethane prepolymer caused by its increased temperature.

3 By increasing the ratio of collagen slurry to urethane prepolymer, the content of collagen fibers in the final sponge was correspondingly increased. The mechanical properties and structure were similar to Examples 1 and 2 above, with slightly increased density noted.
4 This example-was an attempt to add a simple zinc compound to the reaction. The resulting sponge was of much larger cell size than those examples above, and had a significantly greater stiffness. No collagen slurry was used in this reaction. Examples 5-27

While not to be bound by any specific theory, it is believed that the collagen fibers when diluted with water, have a tendency to stretch out and readily absorb any of the biocide, spermicide or other pharmaceutially active agents that are added thereto. Thus, sufficient water is necessarily used with the collagen fibrils in order to prevent the long chains of the collagen from clumping together. Upon sufficien mixing with the urethane prepolymer, or other foam forming polymeric material, the collagen fibers in their extended state are thoroughly dispersed throughout the urethane and upon foaming, the foam tends to encapsulate the collagen fibers containing the pharmaceutically active ingredient. Inasmuch as both the collagen, and the polymeric material are hydrophilic, the resulting structure is an extremely water absorbing foam-type structure which, upon flexing of such foam-type structure, causes the pharmaceutical agent to be released from the collagen fibers and flow out through the various pores in the structure of the foam. This ability to absorb fluids is an important feature for the intravaginal sponge contraceptive application, since by absorbing the semen after ejaculation in the vagina, the amount of sperm available for fertilization can be drastically reduced.

As indicated in Table 1, some of the examples show the use of a heated urethane prepolyer. It has been found that while good results, in terms of good sponge-like structures, are obtained by mixing the urethane with the collagen slurry at room temperature, when the temperature is increased to 110° to about 120°, lower cell density is achieved. A comparison of two identical sponge compositions which varied only in that one used a urethane prepolymer at 110°F before mixing with the collagen slurry while the other used a temperature of 120°F was carried out. The sponge using the urethane prepolymer at 120°F had a retention of over 70% of the amount of pharmaceutically active agents retained after twenty
washings of sponge. The sponge made with the urethane at 110°F, which produced a sponge of a greater density, lost over 50% of the pharmaceutically active agnets after twenty washings. Thus, it has been found that temperature- plays an important role in the ability of the final spong to retain the pharmaceutically active agent therein.

This gave a 20% by dry weight sponge of spermicide and also gave a sponge of good fine cell structure with a lower weight and more resilience than a sponge produced from equal weights of water and polymer.

Example 31 The urethane prepolymer in Example 3 was heated to about 110°F and there was more foaming of the polymer, and a sponge resulted which had slightly larger cells and lower cellular density than the sponge in Example 3.

The resulting sponge was of somewhat lesser weight than the sponge of the previous example and had a slightly finer pore size.
